cultivar: Assam-type Kenyan and Rwandan clones on volcanic soils and drained peat
processing: Mostly CTC, fully oxidised and fired at estate factories fed by smallholder cooperatives; several factories (Sorwathe and Gisovu among them) also make orthodox, green, white and hand-rolled speciality grades.
harvest_season: Year-round; the drier months (June–September and January–February) give the brightest teas.
appearance_dry: Dark granules or, for orthodox, neat twisted black leaf with golden tips.
taste_profile: Bright, brisk and clean with a sweet, lightly fruity malt and more aroma than most East African teas; among the highest-grown tea in Africa.

brewing.notes: The CTC takes milk; orthodox lots are worth drinking plain and give a second steep.

vintage_note: Sold through the Mombasa auction by factory and grade, where Rwandan lots have reached the top of the price list; orthodox and single-estate lots reach speciality shops by factory and year, and a few Rwandan brands pack for export. No vintage: buy the current crop.
description:
Rwanda grows tea on some of the highest and wettest land in Africa, on volcanic slopes and drained peat bogs in the west and north of the country at roughly 1,800 to 2,500 metres. Missionaries are credited with bringing the plant in, commercial plantations followed from the 1950s, and in recent decades Rwandan teas have gone from anonymous blending stock to lots that have reached the top of the price list at the Mombasa auction.

Most of the crop is CTC, fully oxidised and fired at estate factories supplied by smallholder cooperatives, but several factories, Sorwathe at Kinihira and Gisovu above Lake Kivu among them, also make orthodox and speciality grades, including green, white and hand-rolled black teas. Plucking is year-round, with the drier months giving the brightest cups.

The cup is very bright copper-red, brisk and clean, with a sweet, lightly fruity malt and more aroma than most East African teas. Brew it with water just under the boil for three to four minutes; the CTC takes milk, the orthodox lots are worth drinking plain and will give a second steep.

It is sold through the Mombasa auction by factory and grade, and single-estate orthodox lots reach speciality shops by factory and year; a few Rwandan brands also pack for export. No vintage: buy the current crop.

If you want to taste the difference altitude makes in African tea, put a Rwandan next to a Ugandan from the same auction week.
sources_note: Factory locations (Sorwathe at Kinihira, Gisovu near Lake Kivu, Rukeri) from memory.
history:
Accounts of how tea reached Rwanda differ. German missionaries are usually credited with introducing the plant in the early twentieth century, while commercial growing dates from the 1950s. One account puts the first plantation in the Mulindi marsh in 1959, with the Mulindi factory built in 1962.

Today the main growing areas include the western districts of Rutsiro, Nyamasheke and Nyabihu, on volcanic soil at high altitude. Black tea is the main product, with some green. Exports reach countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Pakistan and Japan.
